en: The Questions of Milinda,
Chapter on the Buddha, Section on Inference (Anumānapañha)
2. The Question on the Gift of a Rain-Cloak by Gotamī “Venerable Nāgasena, this was indeed said by the Blessed One when he was giving a rain-cloak to his maternal aunt, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
‘Give it to the Saṅgha, Gotamī; when it is given to the Saṅgha, I shall be honored, as will the Saṅgha.’”
"Venerable Nāgasena, why is it that the Tathāgata was not considered burdensome, heavy, or worthy of offerings because of the Jewel of the Saṅgha,
such that when a rain-cloak— spun, plucked, beaten, carded, and woven by his own maternal aunt, and being offered to him personally— he caused it to be given to the Saṅgha?"
If, venerable Nāgasena, the Tathāgata were superior to, greater than, or more distinguished than the Jewel of the Saṅgha,
then the Tathāgata would not have caused his maternal aunt to give to the Saṅgha a rain-cloak that she had herself spun,
herself plucked, and herself beaten; yet because, venerable sir—
“Nāgasena, the Tathāgata does not long for himself nor does he depend upon himself;
therefore, the Tathāgata had his maternal aunt give that rain-cloak to the Saṅgha.

“This too was said, Great King, by the Blessed One when the rain-cloak was being given by his maternal aunt Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī: ‘Give it to the Saṅgha, Gotamī; when it is given to the Saṅgha, I shall be honored as well as the Saṅgha.’”
But that was not because of my own lack of merit or because I am unworthy of offerings; rather, O Great King,
thinking, "In the future, after my passing, the Saṅgha will be honored for the sake of welfare and out of compassion," he spoke thus while extolling my very existing virtues.
“Give it to the Saṅgha, Gotamī; when it is given to the Saṅgha, both I and the Saṅgha will be honored.

Great King, it is just as when a father, while still living, proclaims his son’s existing virtues in the presence of the king, amidst his ministers, soldiers, guards, gatekeepers, military commanders, and courtiers, saying: “He stands here for the sake of the future.”
‘He will be honored in the midst of the people.

In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata, for the sake of benefit and out of compassion, thinking that after his passing the Saṅgha will be held in high esteem during future times, spoke thus while proclaiming only those qualities that actually exist:
‘Give to the Saṅgha, Gotamī; when you have given to the Saṅgha, I myself and the Saṅgha will both be honored.’”
"Indeed, Great King, the Saṅgha does not become superior or distinguished from the Tathāgata merely by the gift of a rain-cloak.
Just as, Great King, parents anoint, massage, bathe, and rub their children— would the child, Great King, [be considered superior] merely by that much anointing, massaging, bathing, and rubbing?"
“Is he indeed superior or more distinguished than his mother and father?
“No, venerable sir; children cannot act against the will of their parents, venerable sir, which is why parents provide their children with anointing, massaging, bathing, and rubbing.
“In the same way, great king, the Saṅgha does not become superior or more distinguished than the Tathāgata merely by the gift of a rainy-season robe.”
Moreover, the Tathāgata, acting without being subject to personal whims, had that rain-cloak given to the Saṅgha by his maternal aunt.
Or suppose, Great King, a certain man were to bring a gift for the king, and the king were to give that gift to some soldier, or a member of the army, or a general, or a court priest.
Would that man, Great King, on account of merely receiving such a gift, be called superior or distinguished by the king? “No, indeed, Sir.”
“Certainly not, venerable sir. That man is a recipient of the king’s provisions, venerable sir; he subsists on the king. It is because he occupies that position that the king gives him a gift.

“In the same way, great king, the Saṅgha does not become superior or distinguished from the Tathāgata merely by the fact of being presented with a rainy-season robe. Rather, the Saṅgha is a recipient of the Tathāgata’s provisions and subsists on the Tathāgata.
It is because it occupies that position that the Tathāgata caused the Saṅgha to be given a rainy-season robe.”
Moreover, Great King, it occurred to the Tathāgata: "The Saṅgha is worthy of worship by its very nature;
I shall honor the Saṅgha with what belongs to me. Thus he had a rain-cloak given to the Saṅgha. Great King, the Tathāgata does not praise only his own worship;
rather, the Tathāgata [praises] those in the world who are worthy of worship as well.
He praises honoring [the Sangha].

This was also spoken, Great King, by the Blessed One, the God-Beyond-Gods, in the *Dhammadāyāda* discourse within the excellent collection of the *Majjhima Nikāya*, while extolling the practice of fewness of desires:
"That first monk is indeed more worthy of honor and more praiseworthy than I."

"Great King, among all beings in any state of existence, there is no being who is more worthy of offerings than the Tathāgata, nor any who is superior, greater, or more distinguished; the Tathāgata alone is superior, greater, and more distinguished.
This was said, Great King, by the divine son Māṇavagāmika while standing before the Blessed One in the midst of gods and humans in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya:
'Vipula [is the best] of those from Rājagaha...'"
The best of mountains is called the Himalayas; the White Mountain is the best of the Himavat range;
and the sun is the best among those that move through the sky.
The ocean is the best of bodies of water,
and the moon is the best of the constellations;
[so it is] for the world including the devas.
“The Buddha is declared the foremost.
Now, Great King, these verses were well-sung and not poorly sung, well-spoken and not poorly spoken by the young deva Māṇavagāmika, and they were approved by the Blessed One.
Was it not, Great King, also said by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma?
"A single confidence of mind,
or going for refuge, or a salutation with joined palms—
these are sufficient to enable one to cross over."
"To the Buddha who has destroyed Mara’s army.

And it was said by the Blessed One, the God of Gods: "Bhikkhus, one person, appearing in the world, appears for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
What is that one person?"
“The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One...
[as before] ...of gods and humans.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.”
The second question: The Story of Gotamī’s Gift of Cloth.
